timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So I got access to a Linux server with a regular user account. Now what?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Now you escalate privileges, Peter. The goal is to become root. There are two main paths: find a misconfiguration you can exploit, or find a kernel vulnerability.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: SUID binaries are the classic one. Find binaries with the SUID bit set that run as root. If you can make them execute arbitrary commands - like finding a SUID vim or nano - you can read or write any file as root. The command: find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Sudo misconfigurations are even easier. Run 'sudo -l' to see what commands you can run as root. If you can run vim, awk, or even nmap as root, there are well-known techniques to spawn a root shell.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Dirty Pipe - CVE-2022-0847 - was a game-changer. Any local user could overwrite any file on Linux, even root-owned files. Dirty COW was similar. These are unpatched on many systems. Tools like Linux Exploit Suggester automate finding vulnerable kernels.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: On Windows, it's similar. Unquoted service paths, writable service executables, AlwaysInstallElevated registry keys, and token impersonation. Tools like WinPEAS and PowerUp automate the search.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: How do you defend against all this?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Patch systems regularly. Audit SUID binaries - remove unnecessary ones. Follow least privilege with sudo. Use AppArmor or SELinux to restrict what even root can do. And monitor for privilege escalation with EDR.
